title: "Practical 3 — From fixes to trajectories"
subtitle: "Session 3 · Data cleaning, bursts, resampling"
date-modified: last-modified
---



::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Build a trajectory in `amt` and in `adehabitatLT`; clean it and
count what you remove; quantify and visualise sampling irregularity; resample
by selection and by interpolation and see the difference; label day and
night; attach NDVI matched to the time of each fix.

**Time:** ~75 minutes. **Packages:** `amt`, `adehabitatLT`, `terra`, `dplyr`,
`tidyr`, `lubridate`, `ggplot2`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(amt)
library(adehabitatLT)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)
```
:::


## Task 1 — Build a track


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
raw <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(
    id = individual.local.identifier,
    t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
    x  = location.long,
    y  = location.lat
  )

nrow(raw)
#> [1] 28410
```
:::


Now clean, **counting every step**. This block is the template for every
dataset you will ever handle.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n0 <- nrow(raw)

clean <- raw |> filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y))
n1 <- nrow(clean)

clean <- clean |> filter(!(x == 0 & y == 0))
n2 <- nrow(clean)

clean <- clean |> distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)
n3 <- nrow(clean)

data.frame(
  step = c("raw", "drop missing coords", "drop (0,0)", "drop duplicate id+time"),
  rows = c(n0, n1, n2, n3),
  removed = c(NA, n0 - n1, n1 - n2, n2 - n3)
)
#>                     step  rows removed
#> 1                    raw 28410      NA
#> 2    drop missing coords 28410       0
#> 3             drop (0,0) 28410       0
#> 4 drop duplicate id+time 24663    3747
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## Always produce this table

It goes in your methods section, and it is the first thing a reviewer — or a
future you — will want. "We removed 3,747 duplicated records (13.2%)" is a
sentence you can defend. "We cleaned the data" is not.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

trk
#> # A tibble: 24,663 × 4
#>         x_       y_ t_                  id   
#>  *   <dbl>    <dbl> <dttm>              <chr>
#>  1 375051. 7285726. 2005-02-17 05:05:00 Queen
#>  2 374851. 7285502. 2005-02-17 06:08:00 Queen
#>  3 374527. 7284538. 2005-02-17 07:05:00 Queen
#>  4 374492. 7284644. 2005-02-17 08:05:00 Queen
#>  5 374392. 7284667. 2005-02-17 09:05:00 Queen
#>  6 374378. 7284668. 2005-02-17 10:05:00 Queen
#>  7 374422. 7284666. 2005-02-17 11:05:00 Queen
#>  8 374430. 7284663. 2005-02-17 12:05:00 Queen
#>  9 374426. 7284662. 2005-02-17 13:05:00 Queen
#> 10 374733. 7284627. 2005-02-17 14:05:00 Queen
#> # ℹ 24,653 more rows
```
:::


### Your turn

**1a.** What class is `trk`? What are its columns called?
**1b.** Confirm the coordinates are now metres.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
class(trk)
#> [1] "track_xyt"  "track_xy"   "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
names(trk)
#> [1] "x_" "y_" "t_" "id"
summary(trk$x_)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  356761  375417  379046  380566  386182  434568
```
:::


`track_xyt` — a tibble with `x_`, `y_`, `t_` plus the columns you carried
along. The coordinates are now six-figure eastings and seven-figure northings:
UTM 36S metres.
:::

## Task 1b — The same trajectory as an `ltraj`

`adehabitatLT` stores a trajectory as a list of bursts, with the step
descriptors already computed.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cilla <- trk |> filter(id == "Cilla")

ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(cilla[, c("x_", "y_")]),
                date = cilla$t_, id = "Cilla")
ltr
#> 
#> *********** List of class ltraj ***********
#> 
#> Type of the traject: Type II (time recorded)
#> * Time zone: UTC *
#> Irregular traject. Variable time lag between two locs
#> 
#> Characteristics of the bursts:
#>      id burst nb.reloc NAs          date.begin            date.end
#> 1 Cilla Cilla     3528   0 2005-07-14 04:35:00 2005-12-07 22:16:00
#> 
#> 
#>  infolocs provided. The following variables are available:
#> [1] "pkey"

head(ld(ltr)[, c("date", "dist", "dt", "R2n", "abs.angle", "rel.angle")])
#>                  date       dist   dt       R2n  abs.angle rel.angle
#> 1 2005-07-14 04:35:00 13386.3440 3600         0  0.9006608        NA
#> 2 2005-07-14 05:35:00  3943.3528 7200 179194206  2.3910145 1.4903537
#> 3 2005-07-14 07:35:00   817.9605 3540 203227744 -2.1217678 1.7704030
#> 4 2005-07-14 08:34:00   593.9637 3660 180873970 -1.2480422 0.8737256
#> 5 2005-07-14 09:35:00   814.8749 3600 169047094  1.2209400 2.4689822
#> 6 2005-07-14 10:35:00  2097.6577 3540 190861649  2.3937138 1.1727738
```
:::


`dist` is step length (m), `dt` the interval (s), `R2n` the squared distance
from the first fix (we use it in Session 4), and `rel.angle` the turning angle.

### Your turn

**1c.** Compute step lengths and turning angles with `amt` and check they
agree with the `ltraj` columns.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
st_cilla <- cilla |> steps()
c(amt_median_sl = median(st_cilla$sl_),
  ltraj_median_dist = median(ld(ltr)$dist, na.rm = TRUE))
#>     amt_median_sl ltraj_median_dist 
#>          149.4087          149.4087

# amt's ta_ and adehabitat's rel.angle are the same quantity
a <- st_cilla$ta_[-1]
b <- ld(ltr)$rel.angle[2:nrow(st_cilla)]
both <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)

naive    <- max(abs(a[both] - b[both]))                       # plain subtraction
circular <- max(abs(atan2(sin(a[both] - b[both]),             # difference on
                          cos(a[both] - b[both]))))           # the circle
c(compared = sum(both), naive_max_diff = naive, circular_max_diff = circular,
  NA_in_amt = sum(is.na(a)), NA_in_adehabitat = sum(is.na(b)))
#>          compared    naive_max_diff circular_max_diff         NA_in_amt 
#>      3.516000e+03      6.283185e+00      8.881784e-16      1.000000e+01 
#>  NA_in_adehabitat 
#>      5.000000e+00
```
:::


Two lessons in one table.

**Angles are circular.** Plain subtraction reports a maximum difference of
exactly 2π — one package wrote a U-turn as +π, the other as −π, which are the
same direction. Measured on the circle the difference is zero. Never compare,
average or subtract angles as ordinary numbers.

**Undefined angles.** The packages disagree on how many turns to leave
undefined around **zero-length steps**: a step of 0 m has no direction, so the
turn into or out of it cannot be computed. `amt` blanks more of them than
`adehabitatLT` does. Worth knowing before you compare turning-angle
distributions across packages.

Otherwise: same numbers, different containers. Use whichever the next analysis needs:
`ltraj` for first-passage time and Brownian bridges (Sessions 4 and 6), `amt`
for resampling and step selection.
:::

## Task 2 — Sampling rate


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trk |>
  summarize_sampling_rate_many(cols = "id", time_unit = "hour") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(z) round(z, 2)))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 10
#>   id       min    q1 median  mean    q3   max    sd     n unit 
#>   <chr>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 Queen   0.03     1      1  2.45  1    2523. 50.5   4544 hour 
#> 2 Gabs    0.03     1      1  1.22  1     723. 12.0   3669 hour 
#> 3 Cilla   0.05     1      1  1     1       2   0.05  3527 hour 
#> 4 Mvubu   0.03     1      1  0.99  1       9   0.2   2571 hour 
#> 5 Toni    0.08     1      1  1.01  1      17   0.26  5776 hour 
#> 6 Pepper  0.02     1      1  2.47  1.98 1603. 24.6   4570 hour
```
:::


### Your turn

**2a.** What is the programmed fix interval?
**2b.** Why is the mean so much larger than the median?
**2c.** Which individual has the worst gap, and how long is it in days?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

The **median is 1 hour** for every animal — that is the schedule. The mean is
inflated by a handful of enormous gaps:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
gaps <- trk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  arrange(t_, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(dt_h = as.numeric(difftime(t_, lag(t_), units = "hours"))) |>
  ungroup()

gaps |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(
    median_dt = median(dt_h, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_dt   = round(mean(dt_h, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    max_gap_days = round(max(dt_h, na.rm = TRUE) / 24, 1),
    gaps_over_1d = sum(dt_h > 24, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   id     median_dt mean_dt max_gap_days gaps_over_1d
#>   <chr>      <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>        <int>
#> 1 Cilla          1     1            0.1            0
#> 2 Gabs           1     1.2         30.1            2
#> 3 Mvubu          1     1            0.4            0
#> 4 Pepper         1     2.5         66.8           40
#> 5 Queen          1     2.4        105.             9
#> 6 Toni           1     1            0.7            0
```
:::


Always report the **median**. A mean sampling interval is a summary of your
collar failures, not of your sampling design.
:::

## Task 3 — Hunt the speed outliers

First, look. Then delete.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
steps_raw <- trk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  arrange(t_, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    dt_h = as.numeric(difftime(t_, lag(t_), units = "hours")),
    dist_m = sqrt((x_ - lag(x_))^2 + (y_ - lag(y_))^2),
    speed_kmh = (dist_m / 1000) / dt_h
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(speed_kmh))

summary(steps_raw$speed_kmh)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#>  0.00000  0.03129  0.15101  0.29545  0.38204 63.10252
sum(steps_raw$speed_kmh > 15)
#> [1] 4
```
:::


### Your turn

**3a.** Look at the fastest steps. Are they *long* or are they *brief*?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
steps_raw |>
  slice_max(speed_kmh, n = 10) |>
  transmute(id, t_, dt_min = round(dt_h * 60, 1),
            dist_m = round(dist_m), speed_kmh = round(speed_kmh))
#> # A tibble: 10 × 5
#>    id     t_                  dt_min dist_m speed_kmh
#>  * <chr>  <dttm>               <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 Toni   2006-04-20 19:10:00     60  63103        63
#>  2 Toni   2006-04-20 18:10:00     61  63067        62
#>  3 Pepper 2006-05-24 05:06:00     60  17379        17
#>  4 Pepper 2006-05-24 06:07:00     61  16804        17
#>  5 Cilla  2005-07-14 05:35:00     60  13386        13
#>  6 Queen  2005-09-15 07:41:00     70  11783        10
#>  7 Pepper 2006-05-23 15:06:00     60   9898        10
#>  8 Queen  2006-05-26 04:16:00      2    314         9
#>  9 Pepper 2005-10-21 23:02:00      3    255         5
#> 10 Queen  2005-03-26 00:00:00     60   4728         5
```
:::


The worst offenders have **tiny time gaps**, not large distances — a couple of
hundred metres over a minute or two. These are near-duplicate transmissions
that survived the exact-duplicate filter.

Confirm it across all the fast steps:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fast <- steps_raw |> filter(speed_kmh > 15)
summary(fast$dt_h * 60)     # minutes
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    60.0    60.0    60.5    60.5    61.0    61.0
summary(fast$dist_m)        # metres
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   16804   17235   40223   40088   63076   63103
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(steps_raw$dt_h * 60, steps_raw$speed_kmh, log = "xy",
     pch = 16, cex = 0.25, col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.25),
     xlab = "Time gap (minutes, log)", ylab = "Speed km/h (log)",
     main = "Fast steps are short-interval steps")
abline(h = 15, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=624}
:::
:::


The diagonal edge is the signature: apparent speed is bounded by
(GPS error)/dt, so as dt shrinks, apparent speed explodes. **This is a time
problem masquerading as a speed problem** — and deleting the "fast" fixes
would remove perfectly good locations.

The correct remedy is to resample onto a regular grid, which is Task 4.
:::

## Task 4 — Resample into bursts

This is where almost everyone writes a silent bug. Try the obvious thing first.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The "obvious" pipeline — grouped by individual
naive <- trk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
  filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3) |>
  ungroup()

nrow(trk)
#> [1] 24663
nrow(naive)
#> [1] 10395
naive |> count(id, name = "kept")
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   id      kept
#>   <chr>  <int>
#> 1 Cilla   2731
#> 2 Gabs    1921
#> 3 Mvubu    166
#> 4 Pepper   644
#> 5 Queen   1741
#> 6 Toni    3192
```
:::


::: {.callout-important}
## `track_resample()` does not respect `group_by()`

Look at the per-animal counts. Mvubu goes from 2,572 fixes to a couple of
hundred — but Mvubu's data are *fine*: 98.8% of that animal's intervals are
within 10 minutes of one hour.

`track_resample()` walks the rows in time order and builds one grid across
**everything you hand it**. With six animals interleaved, fixes from animal B
fall between the grid points of animal A, and most of the track is discarded.
No error. No warning. Just a much smaller dataset.
:::

The documented `amt` idiom is to split, resample each animal separately, and
recombine:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyr)

trk_hr <- trk |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) {
    d |>
      track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
      filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)
  })) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

nrow(trk_hr)
#> [1] 22828
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trk |> count(id, name = "before") |>
  left_join(naive   |> count(id, name = "grouped_WRONG"), by = "id") |>
  left_join(trk_hr  |> count(id, name = "nested_right"), by = "id") |>
  mutate(pct_kept = round(100 * nested_right / before, 1))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   id     before grouped_WRONG nested_right pct_kept
#> * <chr>   <int>         <int>        <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 Cilla    3528          2731         3518     99.7
#> 2 Gabs     3670          1921         3562     97.1
#> 3 Mvubu    2572           166         2544     98.9
#> 4 Pepper   4571           644         3086     67.5
#> 5 Queen    4545          1741         4354     95.8
#> 6 Toni     5777          3192         5764     99.8
```
:::


Now we keep ~93% of the fixes, which is what an hourly schedule with
occasional failures should give.

### Your turn

**4a.** Recompute speeds on the correctly resampled track. Did the problem go away?
**4b.** What happens if you set `tolerance = minutes(1)`?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
st <- trk_hr |> steps_by_burst()

summary(as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "mins"))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>      54      60      60      60      60      70

sp <- (st$sl_ / 1000) / as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "hours")
round(quantile(sp, c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, 1)), 2)
#>   50%   90%   99% 99.9%  100% 
#>  0.15  0.73  1.93  3.05 63.10
sum(sp > 15)
#> [1] 4
```
:::


Every step now spans 50–70 minutes, and the **time-artefact** speeds are gone:
the median is a few hundred metres per hour, which is what a buffalo does.

But a handful of steps remain absurdly fast. These are different animals
entirely — look at them:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
st[sp > 15, c("t1_", "sl_", "dt_")] |> head(5)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   t1_                    sl_ dt_    
#> * <dttm>               <dbl> <drtn> 
#> 1 2006-04-20 17:09:00 63067. 61 mins
#> 2 2006-04-20 18:10:00 63103. 60 mins
#> 3 2006-05-24 04:06:00 17379. 60 mins
#> 4 2006-05-24 05:06:00 16804. 61 mins
```
:::


Sixty-five **kilometres** in an hour. That is not a short time gap; it is a
genuine spatial outlier — a corrupt fix that teleported the animal and back.
Now that every step spans the same interval, a fast step really does mean a
long distance, and a speed filter finally does what you meant it to do.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "mins"), sp, log = "y", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
     col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.3),
     xlab = "Step duration (minutes)", ylab = "Speed km/h (log)",
     main = "After resampling: fast = far, not brief")
abline(h = 15, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=624}
:::
:::


Compare this with the plot in Task 3: the diagonal artefact edge has gone, and
what is left above the line is a small, isolated cluster of real errors.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tight <- trk |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) d |>
    track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(1)) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3))) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

c(tolerance_10min = nrow(trk_hr), tolerance_1min = nrow(tight))
#> tolerance_10min  tolerance_1min 
#>           22828           21903
```
:::


A tight tolerance discards fixes that arrived a few minutes late — real data
you would rather keep. A loose one lets "hourly" steps range from 40 to 80
minutes, weakening every step-length comparison. 5–10% of the interval is a
reasonable compromise; state whichever you chose.
:::

## Task 5 — Now try the bats


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bat <- read.csv("data/bat_safi.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

bat_trk <- make_track(bat, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32632)     # UTM 32N, Switzerland

bat_trk |>
  summarize_sampling_rate_many(cols = "id", time_unit = "min") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(z) round(z, 1))) |>
  head(8)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 10
#>      id   min    q1 median  mean    q3   max    sd     n unit 
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1    21   1.7   5.2      9 116.   18.8 1605   354.   126 min  
#> 2   289   0.1   6        9 127.   18   1623   372.   161 min  
#> 3   127   0.1   7.2     10 114.   21.8 1448.  344.   114 min  
#> 4   570   0.1   7       11 150.   26   1445.  394.    95 min  
#> 5   146  10    10       10  89.7  12.5 1260   299.    32 min  
#> 6    42  10    10       10 110    10   1310   345.    26 min  
#> 7   168   8     8        8  88.9  10   2764   372.   164 min  
#> 8   495   8     8        8 142.   10   4246   591.   103 min
```
:::


### Your turn

**5a.** Try to resample the bats to a regular 15-minute interval. What survives?
**5b.** What would you do instead?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bat_15 <- bat_trk |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) d |>
    track_resample(rate = minutes(15), tolerance = minutes(5)) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3))) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

c(before = nrow(bat_trk), after = nrow(bat_15))
#> before  after 
#>   1740    802

bursts <- bat_15 |> count(id, burst_)
c(n_bursts = nrow(bursts), median_length = median(bursts$n), max_length = max(bursts$n))
#>      n_bursts median_length    max_length 
#>           165             4            13
table(bursts$n)
#> 
#>  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 10 11 13 
#> 57 34 26 20  8  7  5  4  2  2
```
:::


Fewer than half the fixes survive — but the real problem is the *shape* of
what is left. The 802 surviving fixes shatter into **165 bursts with a median
length of 4**, i.e. three steps each. There is no programmed schedule to
recover: fixes arrived whenever a field worker obtained a bearing.

A hidden Markov model (Session 8) estimates *transition* probabilities between
behavioural states. With bursts of three steps, there is almost nothing to
transition — you would be asking the model to learn the dynamics of a process
from fragments shorter than the process itself.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
lags <- bat_trk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  arrange(t_, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(dt_min = as.numeric(difftime(t_, lag(t_), units = "mins"))) |>
  ungroup() |> filter(!is.na(dt_min), dt_min > 0)

hist(log10(lags$dt_min), breaks = 40, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     xlab = "log10 interval (minutes)", main = "Bat sampling intervals span five orders of magnitude")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](exercise_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


**What to do instead.** Not: force a regular grid and pretend. The honest
options are

- restrict to the questions these data *can* answer — which sites were used,
  broad home-range extent, night-time activity periods;
- use methods that tolerate irregular sampling, i.e. **continuous-time**
  models (`ctmm`) rather than discrete-step models;
- treat each night as a separate short burst and analyse only within-night
  movement.

Recognising which of your datasets is a "buffalo" and which is a "bat" is one
of the more valuable things you will take from this course.
:::

## Task 6 — Interpolation is not resampling

`adehabitatLT::redisltraj()` also produces a regular hourly series — by
inventing positions.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cilla_ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(cilla[, c("x_", "y_")]),
                      date = cilla$t_, id = "Cilla")
interp <- redisltraj(cilla_ltr, 3600, type = "time")

selected <- trk_hr |> filter(id == "Cilla")

c(original_fixes = nrow(cilla),
  selected_by_track_resample = nrow(selected),
  produced_by_redisltraj = nrow(ld(interp)))
#>             original_fixes selected_by_track_resample 
#>                       3528                       3518 
#>     produced_by_redisltraj 
#>                       3522
```
:::


### Your turn

**6a.** How many of the interpolated positions coincide with a real fix?
**6b.** What would interpolated positions do to a step-length distribution?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
real_times <- cilla$t_
interp_times <- ld(interp)$date
sum(interp_times %in% real_times)
#> [1] 30
length(interp_times)
#> [1] 3522
```
:::


Almost none of the "hourly" positions is an observation: `redisltraj()` walks
along the straight lines between fixes and places a point every 3,600 seconds.
Every one of those points assumes the animal moved at constant speed in a
straight line between fixes.

Consequences: step lengths across a gap become artificially uniform, turning
angles on interpolated stretches become exactly zero, and any model fitted to
them sees a smooth, persistent animal that never existed. Use interpolation
for **display**, never as data — or use a model that interpolates with
uncertainty (`ctmm`, `crawl`), which is what Sessions 6 and 8 do.
:::

## Task 7 — Day or night?

Many behaviours are diel. `time_of_day()` labels each fix from the sun's
position at that place and time.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cilla_tod <- selected |>
  time_of_day()

cilla_steps <- cilla_tod |>
  steps_by_burst(keep_cols = "start")

cilla_steps |>
  group_by(tod_) |>
  summarise(steps = n(), median_sl_m = round(median(sl_)),
            mean_sl_m = round(mean(sl_)))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   tod_  steps median_sl_m mean_sl_m
#>   <fct> <int>       <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 day    1801         221       347
#> 2 night  1714         104       218
```
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What this shows

Buffalo move further per hour by day than by night — a diel pattern you must
account for before interpreting anything else about their movement. In Session
8 we let the probability of switching behavioural state depend on the time of
day.
:::

## Task 8 — NDVI matched to the time of each fix

The NDVI raster from Session 2 has two layers, a wet-season composite (2 Feb
2005) and a dry-season one (14 Sep 2005). Tell `terra` when each was taken,
then let `amt` give every fix the value of the composite closest in time.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ndvi <- project(rast("data/kruger_ndvi_2005.tif"), "EPSG:32736")
time(ndvi) <- as.POSIXct(c("2005-02-02", "2005-09-14"), tz = "UTC")
ndvi
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 504, 445, 2  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 258.5037, 258.5037  (x, y)
#> extent      : 338541.4, 453575.6, 7215872, 7346158  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : WGS 84 / UTM zone 36S (EPSG:32736)
#> source(s)   : memory

#> max values  :        0.804637,        0.583936

queen <- trk |> filter(id == "Queen", year(t_) == 2005)

queen_ndvi <- queen |>
  extract_covariates_var_time(ndvi, when = "any", max_time = days(45),
                              name_covar = "ndvi")

queen_ndvi |>
  mutate(month = month(t_, label = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(fixes = n(), with_ndvi = sum(!is.na(ndvi)),
            mean_ndvi = round(mean(ndvi, na.rm = TRUE), 3))
```

:::


### Your turn

**8a.** Why are most months `NA`? **8b.** What would you need to annotate the
whole year?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

With `max_time = days(45)`, a fix is annotated only if a composite exists
within 45 days of it. We have two composites, so only February–March and
September–October are covered. Everything else is honestly `NA` — far better than
silently assigning February's greenness to a July fix.

To annotate the whole year you need the full series: MOD13Q1 produces a
composite every 16 days, 23 per year. The same `MODISTools` call that built
this file fetches them all — it just takes longer:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(MODISTools)
ndvi_ts <- mt_subset(product = "MOD13Q1", band = "250m_16_days_NDVI",
                     lat = -24.58, lon = 31.97, km_lr = 45, km_ab = 70,
                     start = "2005-01-01", end = "2006-12-31")
ndvi_ts <- mt_to_terra(ndvi_ts, reproject = TRUE)   # already scaled to NDVI units
```
:::


Or upload the track to Movebank's **Env-DATA**, which does the matching and the
temporal interpolation for you. Either way, check the result with `summary()`:
NDVI must lie between −1 and 1. If you see values in the thousands, the scale
factor was not applied; if you see values a thousand times too small, it was
applied twice.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
Which cleaning order is correct?

- [ ] Speed filter → remove duplicates → resample
- [x] Remove duplicates → resample to a regular rate → inspect remaining outliers
- [ ] Resample → remove duplicates → speed filter
- [ ] The order does not matter

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Duplicates and near-duplicates create tiny time gaps, and tiny time gaps
create enormous apparent speeds. Filter on speed first and you delete good
fixes for a fault that belongs to their neighbours.

Remove duplicates, then resample so that every step spans a comparable
interval, and *then* look at what is still implausible. By that point, a
genuinely fast step really is a long distance.
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
You pipe six animals into `group_by(id) |> track_resample(rate = hours(1))`
and keep 42% of your fixes. The same animals resampled one at a time keep 93%.
Why?

- [x] `track_resample()` ignores `group_by()` and builds one time grid across all animals
- [ ] `group_by()` removed the duplicate timestamps
- [ ] The tolerance was too tight
- [ ] 42% is correct; the per-animal version double-counts

::: {.quiz-feedback}
`track_resample()` walks the rows in time order and lays a single regular grid
over whatever you give it. Hand it six interleaved animals and most fixes fall
between grid points set by some *other* individual, so they are dropped.

It fails silently — no error, no warning, just a smaller dataset — which is
what makes it dangerous. Use the `nest()` / `lapply()` / `unnest()` idiom so
each animal gets its own grid.

**The general lesson:** not every function respects `dplyr` grouping. When a
step drops far more data than you expected, check the per-group counts before
you accept the result.
:::
